The second bit of humility we'll end the class on is I am presenting here, and I'll be presenting throughout this semester, what you can call a mechanistic conception of mental life. I'm not going to be talking about how beautiful it is and how wonderful it is and how mysterious it is. Rather, I'm going to be trying to explain it. I'm going to be trying to explain fundamental aspects of ourselves including questions like how do we make decisions, why do we love our children, what happens when we fall in love, and so on. Now, you might find this sort of project in the end to be repellant. You might worry about how this, well, this meshes with humanist values. For instance, when we deal with one another in a legal and a moral setting, we think in terms of free will and responsibility. If we're driving and you cut me off, you chose to do that. It reflects badly on you. If you save a life at risk to your own, you're--you deserve praise. You did something wonderful. It might be hard to mesh this with the conception in which all actions are the result of neurochemical physical processes. It might also be hard to mesh a notion such as the purported intrinsic value of people. And finally, it might be hard to mesh the mechanistic notion of the mind with the idea that people have spiritual value.

questions.q: A driver cuts you off and you blame them for choosing to do it. Why might the mechanistic view make this blame seem puzzling?
options: Because if all actions result from neurochemical processes, it is hard to fit the idea that they freely chose
questions.explanation: Bloom says free will and responsibility are hard to mesh with a view in which all actions result from neurochemical physical processes.

questions.q: What does Bloom mean by a "mechanistic conception of mental life"?
options: Believing the soul controls the brain
Trying to explain mental life, like decisions and love, as physical processes
Treating the mind as mysterious and beautiful
questions.explanation: He says he won't dwell on how mysterious it is; he'll try to explain fundamental aspects of ourselves.

concept: Three responses to the tension between science and humanist values
summary: Faced with this tension, you can reject the scientific conception of mind and embrace dualism, or embrace science and reject free will, responsibility and spiritual value as illusions. Or you can try to reconcile the scientific view of the mind with the humanist values you want to preserve, an issue the course returns to throughout.
text: Faced with this tension, there are three possibilities. You might choose to reject the scientific conception of the mind. Many people do. You may choose to embrace dualism, reject the idea that the brain is responsible for mental life, and reject the promise of a scientific psychology. Alternatively, you might choose to embrace the scientific worldview and reject all these humanist values. And there are some philosophers and psychologists who do just that, who claim that free will and responsibility and spiritual value and intrinsic value are all illusions; they're pre-scientific notions that get washed away in modern science or you could try to reconcile them. You could try to figure out how to mesh your scientific view of the mind with these humanist values you might want to preserve. And this is an issue which we're going to return to throughout the course.

questions.q: A philosopher argues that neuroscience is right and that free will is simply a pre-scientific illusion. Which of Bloom's three responses is this?
options: Embrace the scientific view and reject humanist values
questions.explanation: Bloom describes philosophers and psychologists who claim free will and responsibility are illusions washed away by science.

questions.q: Someone accepts that the mind is the brain but still wants to keep moral responsibility. Which response are they attempting?
options: Reconciling the scientific view with humanist values
questions.explanation: The third option is to try to mesh the scientific view of the mind with the humanist values you want to preserve.
